metadata.title: Wait—Git Never Stores Diffs?! Here’s What It Stores Instead 🤯 #Shorts
metadata.description: Ever wondered why Git doesn’t save “diffs” like most version tools? The hook: Git stores content as snapshots of files, then uses hashing + compression to avoid duplicates—so history stays fast and storage stays efficient. Under the hood, each commit points to a tree of file states, and blobs are shared across versions via their hashes. Understanding this snapshot model helps you reason about merges, performance, and why Git is so reliable at scale. Follow @kreggscode and drop your question in the comments—what part of Git do you want decoded next?

metadata.title: Python’s GIL Explained: Why One Core Can’t Run Your Code Faster #Shorts
metadata.description: Ever wondered why Python threads don’t always speed up your program? The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is a runtime mechanism that ensures only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. That design makes Python simpler and safer, but it can limit CPU-bound concurrency—especially for multi-threaded workloads. In this video, we break down what the GIL is, when it matters, and how to work around it with multiprocessing or native extensions. Follow @kreggscode and drop your questions in the comments!

metadata.title: 0.1 + 0.2 Isn’t 0.3 in Code—Here’s Why (and How to Fix It) #Shorts
metadata.description: Ever added 0.1 + 0.2 and got 0.30000000000000004? That’s the classic floating-point rounding problem—small enough to seem harmless, but dangerous in real systems like billing, money, and comparisons. Computers store decimals in binary, so many “simple” numbers can’t be represented exactly, causing tiny errors that accumulate. In this short, we’ll show why it happens and the practical ways to avoid it (like rounding or using integers). Follow @kreggscode and comment: what bug have floating-point errors caused for you?

metadata.title: Why QR Codes Still Work When Torn—Error Correction Explained! #Shorts
metadata.description: Ever wonder how a QR code can be ripped or smudged and still scan? The secret is error correction: QR codes include redundant data so the decoder can reconstruct missing or damaged bits. In computer science terms, it’s like coding theory in action—designing for noisy, real-world data streams. Understanding these ideas helps you build more reliable systems, from storage to network communication. Follow @kreggscode and comment: what kind of error correction should we break down next?

metadata.title: Puncture a Li-ion Battery → instant fire? Here’s the code-level chemistry #Shorts
metadata.description: Ever wonder why a “simple” puncture can turn a lithium battery into a flame? Lithium-ion cells are like tightly coupled systems—when the seal breaks, internal reactions trigger rapid heating and runaway chemistry. In software terms, it’s the same idea as a cascading failure: one fault bypasses safety checks and the system spirals out of control. Understanding failure modes matters for designing safer products, embedded monitoring, and reliable power management code. metadata.title: Hash Tables Are “O(1)”… Until They Collide 😬 #Shorts
metadata.description: Hash tables look like magic: average lookup/insert is O(1). But collisions happen when two keys map to the same bucket, and suddenly you’re paying extra time. In this video, we’ll break down what causes collisions and how chaining or probing turns “constant time” into worst-case O(n). Want faster intuition for real-world performance? metadata.title: GPUs vs CPUs: Why AI training can be 100x faster (here’s the real reason) #Shorts
metadata.description: Ever wondered why the same neural net trains in hours on a GPU but can take days on a CPU? It’s because GPUs are built for massive parallelism—thousands of cores that run the same math across many data points at once. AI training is mostly repeated matrix operations, and GPUs keep those operations flowing with specialized high-throughput hardware. Understanding this helps you choose the right compute stack and write faster, more efficient code. metadata.title: Binary search trees are slow—why real DBs use B-Trees instead #Shorts
metadata.description: Ever wonder why databases don’t just use a classic binary tree? The answer is about how computers actually store data: B-Trees are designed to minimize disk and cache misses by keeping many keys per node. That means fewer reads, faster range queries, and smoother performance as your dataset grows. If you’re building apps or studying system design, this is a key data-structure insight.
